why: Picking values in chronological order that are strictly increasing, with skips allowed, is exactly the Longest Increasing Subsequence. The financial story (prices or signed monthly profits) changes nothing.
hints: Skipping months is allowed and order must be kept: that is a subsequence, not a subarray.
This is plain LIS with strict increase. dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with value[j] < value[i] works in O(n^2), which already fits n = 2,500.

For O(n log n), keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each value, binary-search the first tail >= it (bisect_left) and replace it, or append. The answer is len(tails).
pitfalls: Strictly increasing: equal values cannot both be picked, so use bisect_left, not bisect_right.
Values can be negative or zero; do not seed anything with 0 as a 'minus infinity'.
tails is not itself a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful.
constraints:
• 1 <= prices.length <= 2500
  • -10^4 <= prices[i] <= 10^4
  • Practice bounds; the source report discusses a size of about 1,000 and gives no value bounds.
